newsitem.title: MEXICO: Investors seen having fragile affair with Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Investors seen having fragile affair with Mexico.

text.p: Mexico has once again aroused the ardor of foreign investors, but financial analysts say the affair may be cut short in the second quarter by political jitters ahead of mid-term elections and economic concerns.

Since the New Year, Mexico's stock, currency and money markets have all rallied, with the help of foreign money chasing the benefits of a fast-recovering economy, strong oil revenues and a stable outlook for the time-being on U.S. interest rates.

So far this year, some $500 million of foreign cash has entered the markets, according to four analysts consulted by Reuters. "Foreign investors are optimistic about the economy," said Diego Candano, chief investment strategist at IXE brokerage, explaining the capital inflows.
In addition to investment, the markets have been awash with liquidity due to higher-than-expected revenues from oil exports, partly due to high world energy prices.
That has helped strengthen the peso by some 9 centavos against the dollar from its 1996 closing level of 7.8950.
"Traditionally (in winter) there are capital inflows to buy energy and agricultural products," said Jaime Hernandez, analyst at Estrategia Asesoria, a Mexican consultancy firm.
"If you add to that the fact that it's been a hard winter, there are additional inflows that have caused the exchange rate to revalue."
But thunder clouds are looming, most analysts say, that could drench the honeymoon at the end of March, putting renewed upward pressure on interest rates and the peso.

"We are seeing a difficult second quarter ahead...I think you've got to be very careful," said Hector Chavez, analyst at Santander Investments, whose chief concern was a possible rise in U.S. interest rates when the Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25.

"It's probable that U.S. interest rates will rise in the second quarter because economic growth will be stronger than expected. With low (interest rates) in Mexico, this could cause a little bit more risk," he said.
Mexico has to pay some $500 million in interest payments on its Brady bonds at the end of the first quarter, further offsetting capital inflows.
And analysts said as winter ends and the temperature rises, demand for Mexican oil will drop cutting prices and lowering revenues.

The economic concerns run in tandem with the fear of increased political tensions ahead of elections in July, and the possibility that President Ernesto Zedillo may have to deal with an opposition Chamber of Deputies afterwards.

In the battle to elect the first-ever non-appointed mayor of Mexico City, the entire chamber of deputies and seven state governors, Mexico's opposition is expected to present a strong challenge to Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party.

At the end of the first quarter, "the elections will be just three months away and people could begin to reshuffle their portfolios and get out of Mexican paper," Hernandez said, even though he and other analysts expected it to be only a temporary retreat.
Analysts expected the political concerns to carry the peso steadily down to nine per dollar by the end of the year, though they doubted it would sink much before April.
The currency would also be pressured by an ongoing assessment of the inflation differentials between Mexico and the United States, they said.
Interest rates, meanwhile, were expected to end the first quarter around 20 or 21 percent, rebounding to about 23 percent by the end of the year, their current level.
